items.prompt: Where does most of a tree's solid wood come from?

options.label: The soil
options.feedback: A tree gains tonnes while the soil around it loses almost nothing. Minerals come from the soil, but not the bulk.

options.label: The water it drinks
options.feedback: Water supplies the hydrogen, but nearly all of it passes through and leaves again through the leaves.

options.label: The air
options.feedback: Carbon pulled out of the air is what the wood is built from.

options.label: The sunlight
options.feedback: Sunlight supplies the energy for the building, not the material. Light has no substance to become wood.

items.ok_line: The wood was gas before it was wood.
items.ko_line: The mistake is to look at the ground the tree stands in rather than the air it stands in.
items.exp_text: A leaf takes carbon dioxide from the air and uses the energy of light to break it apart, keeping the carbon and joining it to water to make sugar. That sugar is the brick: it becomes cellulose, and cellulose becomes wood. So the trunk in front of you is largely carbon that was drifting past as a gas, and the air is where it came from.

items.prompt: Why does a leaf look green?

options.label: Chlorophyll reflects green light
options.feedback: Green is the part chlorophyll cannot use, so it comes back to your eye.

options.label: Chlorophyll absorbs green light
options.feedback: If it absorbed green, that green would never reach your eye and the leaf would look dark.

options.label: Green light carries the most energy
options.feedback: Blue carries more than green, and chlorophyll works best on red and blue. Green sits in the middle, least used of all.

options.label: The plant makes a green dye for shade
options.feedback: Nothing here is made to be seen. The colour is what is left over, not a product.

items.ok_line: You are looking at the light the leaf turned away.
items.ko_line: The colour you see is never the colour a thing absorbs.
items.exp_title: Green is the colour left over
items.exp_text: Chlorophyll absorbs light strongly at the red and the blue ends of the range, and hardly at all in the middle. The light it cannot use is neither stored nor destroyed — it passes through the leaf or bounces off it. What bounces back to your eye is that unused middle, and the middle is green.

items.prompt: How does carbon dioxide get inside a leaf?

options.label: Straight through the waxy surface
options.feedback: The waxy skin exists to stop things crossing, water above all. Gas cannot pass it either.

options.label: Through tiny pores, mostly underneath
options.feedback: Each pore opens onto the air and lets the gas walk in.

options.label: Up from the roots with the water
options.feedback: Roots draw water and minerals. Air trapped in soil never travels to the leaf that way.

options.label: Through the veins from the stem
options.feedback: Veins carry liquid — water one way, sugar the other. They are closed to the air.

items.ok_line: A sealed leaf with openable holes in it.
items.ko_line: Ask which parts of a leaf are actually open to the outside air.
items.exp_title: A door that also loses water
items.exp_text: A leaf is wrapped in a waxy skin that keeps its water in, and the same skin keeps carbon dioxide out. The way round it is a set of pores, each one a gap between two curved cells that swell to open it and slacken to shut it. They sit mostly on the shaded underside, where the air is stiller and less water escapes, and that is where the gas comes in.

items.prompt: What does a plant give off while it is making its food?

options.label: Carbon dioxide
options.feedback: That is what the leaf takes in. A plant does release it as well, but from burning sugar, not from making it.

options.label: Nitrogen
options.feedback: Nitrogen drifts past the leaf untouched. What nitrogen a plant needs comes up from the soil.

options.label: Water vapour only
options.feedback: Water vapour does escape through the pores, but it leaks out — nothing makes it.

options.label: Oxygen
options.feedback: Waste to the plant, and the reason you can breathe.

items.ok_line: One creature's rubbish is another's air.
items.ko_line: Two gases cross the pores in opposite directions. This question asks about the one going out.
items.exp_title: The waste that everything else breathes
items.exp_text: Building sugar needs hydrogen, and the plant gets it by splitting water apart with the energy of light. The hydrogen is kept and joined to carbon taken from the air; what remains has no use in the leaf and is pushed back out through the pores. What remains is oxygen.

items.prompt: Which of the things a plant takes in becomes the oxygen it releases?

options.label: The carbon dioxide
options.feedback: It does contain oxygen, which makes this the natural guess, but those atoms stay behind in the sugar.

options.label: The minerals in the soil
options.feedback: Minerals are needed in small amounts to build particular parts of the plant. None of them leaves as a gas.

options.label: The water
options.feedback: It is torn open for its hydrogen, and its oxygen goes free.

options.label: The light
options.feedback: Light brings energy, not matter. Nothing it delivers can leave again as a gas.

items.ok_line: You tracked the atoms rather than the names.
items.ko_line: Both candidates contain oxygen, so the name of the gas is no help. Follow what happens to each one.
items.exp_text: Carbon dioxide and water both carry oxygen, so from their names either could be the source. The carbon dioxide is taken apart for its carbon alone, and the oxygen that came with it is carried onward into the sugar. The molecule that is broken open and surrenders its oxygen to the air is the water.

items.prompt: What does a plant do with the sugar it makes?

options.label: Builds its body and stores the rest
options.feedback: Some is spent at once, some becomes substance, some is locked away for later.

options.label: Sends all of it to the flowers
options.feedback: Flowers and fruit are expensive and do get a share, but so do the roots, the trunk and every new leaf.

options.label: Turns all of it back into carbon dioxide
options.feedback: That happens to the part the plant burns for energy. The rest becomes the plant.

options.label: Keeps it as sugar inside the leaves
options.feedback: Sugar sitting in a leaf would pull water in and be easily washed away. It is converted into starch, which does neither.

items.ok_line: Fuel, building material and reserve, out of one substance.
items.ko_line: Each wrong answer is one real use mistaken for the only use.
items.exp_text: Sugar is both the plant's fuel and its building material. Part is burned straight away to power growing and repairing; part is rebuilt into cellulose for walls and stems; part is packed into starch, which dissolves in nothing and so stays put until it is wanted. So the sugar builds the plant's body, and what is not needed today is stored.

items.prompt: Why is a leaf flat and thin rather than thick and rounded?

options.label: So rain runs off it quickly
options.feedback: Water does run off a leaf, and the shape helps, but a thick leaf would shed rain just as well.

options.label: So it weighs as little as possible
options.feedback: Weight matters to a branch, yet a thick leaf could still be light. Thinness is bought for something else.

options.label: So it can fold away in bad weather
options.feedback: A few plants do fold their leaves, and they are thin for the same reason every leaf is, not in order to fold.

options.label: To catch light and let gas reach every cell
options.feedback: Two jobs, and both are served by surface rather than depth.

items.ok_line: Flat for the light, thin for the gas.
items.ko_line: Flatness and thinness are two separate answers to two separate problems.
items.exp_text: Light is caught by area, so spreading a given amount of leaf out wide intercepts far more of it than bunching it up. Thinness does the other job: carbon dioxide has to drift in through the pores and reach every working cell, and in a thick leaf the cells in the middle would be starved of it. Flat catches the light, and thin feeds the inside.

items.prompt: Why does a seedling growing under a fallen log come up pale and spindly?

options.label: The log presses it thin
options.feedback: A seedling can lift a surprising weight, and pressure would not drain its colour.

options.label: No light means no chlorophyll, so it stretches
options.feedback: Pale because nothing green was built, long because it is reaching.

options.label: It has run out of water
options.feedback: Thirst makes a plant wilt and shrink rather than stretch, and it stays green while it does.

options.label: It is a different kind of plant
options.feedback: The same seed sown in the open comes up short and green. Only the light has changed.

items.ok_line: The colour and the shape have the same cause.
items.ko_line: Whatever explains the paleness has to explain the stretching too.
items.exp_title: A gamble on reaching the light
items.exp_text: Chlorophyll is costly to build and a plant only builds it where light falls, so a seedling in the dark stays the colour of the food stored in its seed. Meanwhile its growing tip pours everything into length, because that store will run out and height is the only way to reach light before it does. Pale because no light means no chlorophyll, spindly because the only way out is up.

items.prompt: Does a plant use oxygen as well as make it?

options.label: No, only animals use oxygen
options.feedback: Every living cell releases its energy the same way. A plant cell is no exception.

options.label: Only when it is flowering
options.feedback: Flowering is expensive and does need fuel, but the cells were burning it long before any flower appeared.

options.label: Yes, all the time, day and night
options.feedback: Every cell burns sugar, and burning sugar needs oxygen.

options.label: Only at night, never in daylight
options.feedback: It looks that way because in daylight the leaf makes more than the plant burns, so the burning is hidden.

items.ok_line: Making food and living off it are two different things.
items.ko_line: A process you cannot measure from outside is not a process that has stopped.
items.exp_title: It breathes as well as it feeds
items.exp_text: Making sugar and spending sugar are two separate jobs, and a plant does both. Its cells burn sugar with oxygen to release the energy for growing and repairing, exactly as your cells do, and they never pause. In daylight a leaf produces more oxygen than the plant burns, so the burning goes unseen — but it runs at every hour, day and night.

items.prompt: Why does a plant shut its leaf pores on a hot dry day?

options.label: To stop losing water
options.feedback: And it pays dearly, because the food-making stops with them.

options.label: To stop losing sugar
options.feedback: Sugar never leaves by the pores. It travels inside the plant, through the veins.

options.label: To keep the leaf cool
options.feedback: Shutting them does the opposite: escaping water cools a leaf, so a closed leaf runs hotter.

options.label: To stop insects getting in
options.feedback: A pore is far too small for an insect, and a plant has other defences against them.

items.ok_line: Shutting the door keeps the water and stops the food.
items.ko_line: The pores are open to the air, so ask what can escape through them.
items.exp_title: A choice between eating and drinking
items.exp_text: The same opening that lets carbon dioxide in lets water vapour out, and a plant cannot have one without the other. On a dry day the water leaves faster than the roots can replace it, so the guard cells slacken and the pores close. Food-making stops for as long as they stay shut, and the plant accepts that in order to stop losing water.
